title: Infancy, Toddlerhood and Childhood Development
introduction: From a baby's first social smile and pincer grip through the boundary-testing autonomy of the 'terrible twos' and the logical, school-ready mastery of middle childhood, the first twelve years lay the structural, cognitive, and social groundwork for adult competence. Tracking gross and fine motor milestones, core cognitive skills, and socialization processes equips practitioners to detect developmental delays early.
learningOutcomes: 7.1 Distinguish gross motor skills from fine motor skills with concrete developmental examples and explain why hand-eye coordination is a prerequisite for writing.
7.2 Trace month-by-month developmental milestones across Infancy (months 1–12), highlighting major motor, sensory, language, and emotional markers.
7.3 Outline physical, mental, and emotional milestones across Toddlerhood (12–36 months), including the 'terrible twos', toilet training, and vocabulary explosion.

7.4 Compare physical, cognitive, and psychosocial development in Early Childhood (2–6 years) versus Middle Childhood (6–11/13 years), including reticular formation maturation and bilingual cognitive advantages.
7.5 Define the core childhood cognitive skills (attention types, memory, reasoning, auditory/visual processing) and explain socialization and psychosocial treatment interventions.

content.heading: Gross vs. Fine Motor Skills and Infancy Milestones (Months 1–12)
content.body: Physical growth is rapid in the first two years: by age 2, a toddler reaches nearly half of adult height and quadruples birth weight, progressing along cephalocaudal and proximodistal gradients. Motor development advances from Gross Motor Skills (controlling large muscles of trunk, arms, and legs—walking, running, jumping, climbing, pedalling, throwing/catching, balancing, hopping, skipping, gymnastics/dance) to Fine Motor Skills (small muscle coordination for building block towers, puzzles, tying shoelaces, clay/dough modelling, cutting with scissors, sewing, pouring, and computer mouse control—maturing alongside eye muscles into hand-eye coordination, a prerequisite for holding pencils and writing). Key Infancy Milestones (1–12 months): Month 1 (hands to mouth, flinches at loud sounds, focuses within ~12 inches/nearby face, turns to familiar voices); Month 2 (gurgling/cooing, early visual tracking, lifts head/pushes up on tummy); Month 3 (smiles at voice, lifts head/chest prone, grasps toys, vowel sounds 'ooh/ah', imitates expressions); Month 4 (shakes rattle, begins rolling tummy-to-back, pushes legs when held standing); Month 5 (rolls both ways, grabs feet to mouth, transfers hand-to-hand, shows solid-food interest); Month 6 (sits briefly unsupported, consonant/vowel sounds, recognizes own name, expresses anger/joy); Month 7 (sits unsupported longer, responds to 'no', reads emotional tone, raking grasp, strings consonants); Month 8 (rocks on hands/knees, pulls to stand, drooling/first teeth, 'ma-ma/da-da' babbling, stranger/separation anxiety begins); Month 9 (crawls, plays peekaboo/finds hidden objects, Pincer Grip using thumb and forefinger, points); Month 10 (cruising along furniture, bangs objects, container play, finger-foods, shakes head 'no', waves 'bye-bye'); Month 11 (inflected mama/dada/uh-oh, understands 'don't touch', mimics phone calls); Month 12 (stands briefly unsupported/takes 1–2 steps, says 1–2 simple words like hi/no/bye, uses spoon/comb clumsily, looks at named objects).

content.heading: Toddlerhood Milestones (12–36 Months)
content.body: Toddlerhood (12–36 months—when a child learns to 'toddle') is popularly nicknamed the 'terrible twos' due to boundary-testing temper tantrums (which can start as early as 9 months) as toddlers realize they are separate individuals striving for independence—requiring consistent caregiver warmth, communication, and safety boundaries. Toilet training typically begins between 17 months and 3 years depending on readiness, and around 18 months vocabulary explodes at 7–9 new words per day. Age-banded milestones: 12–15 months—Physical (stands well, drinks poorly from cup, turns several pages, tosses ball), Mental (4–6 words, follows gesture-paired commands, Object Permanence for hidden toys), Emotional (gestures/points for desires, mimics covering eyes); 15–18 months—Physical (walks well alone, bends/stands up, scribbles with crayon, climbs furniture), Mental (10–20 words, follows commands without gestures, stacks 2 blocks), Emotional (greets others, mimics cleaning or phone talk); 18–24 months—Physical (spoon-feeds self, runs, climbs small chair, walks up steps), Mental (20–50 words, stacks 6 blocks, understands light switches/buttons, sorts toys, searches for hidden objects, trial-and-error problem-solving), Emotional (asserts independence/'no'/tantrums, feeds doll/hugs teddy, self-recognition, separation anxiety, turn-taking); 24–36 months—Physical (advanced climbing, small-object dexterity, puzzles, dresses self), Mental (speaks in sentences, anticipates routines, imaginative play, sings along), Emotional (distinguishes boys from girls, expresses clothing/entertainment preferences).

content.heading: Early Childhood (2–6 Years), Middle Childhood (6–11/13 Years), Cognitive Skills, and Socialization
content.body: Early Childhood (2–6 years) broadens activity beyond caregivers toward formal schooling: locomotion becomes graceful (3-year-old runs straight and jumps smoothly; 4-year-old skips, hops on one foot, catches large ball; 6-year-old displays coordinated balance), fine motor skills (buttoning shirts, copying figures) surge, and symbolic thought flourishes. Sustained attention lengthens markedly—from 15–20 minutes at age 3 to over 1 hour at age 6—driven partly by maturation of the brain's Reticular Formation (regulating attention through puberty), alongside sharper selective attention and perceptual discrimination. Middle Childhood (6–11/13 years) brings slower, gradual physical growth until the pubertal spurt, quicker reaction time, vigorous action games, and refined small-muscle mastery (6–7-year-olds copy diamonds, assemble models, use tools like screwdrivers). Cognitively, concrete logical thinking strengthens (e.g., 10-year-olds solve arithmetic and concrete inferences but struggle with abstract hypotheticals), memory and hobbies expand, and school-agers internalize gender constancy and sex-role standards. Bilingual or multilingual children exposed to multiple languages exhibit higher cognitive proficiency and language understanding than monolinguals. Core Childhood Cognitive Skills essential for school and lifelong success include: Sustained Attention (staying focused long-term), Selective Attention (ignoring distractions like TV during homework), Divided Attention (multitasking two actions), Long-Term Memory (recalling past formulas/facts), Working Memory (holding instructions while executing them), Logic & Reasoning (problem-solving/idea generation), Auditory Processing (analysing/blending sounds for reading), and Visual Processing (interpreting maps, graphs, tables). Psychosocially, childhood is central to Socialization—learning family and cultural norms through parents, grandparents, adults, and peers. Because childhood behavioural, emotional, and educational disorders are prevalent yet undertreated, early detection by developmental psychologists enables psychosocial treatments including structured counselling, motivational enhancement, case management, care-coordination, psychotherapy, and relapse prevention.

inTextQuestions.question: What distinguishes a 'raking grasp' (7 months) from a 'pincer grip' (9 months) during infancy?
inTextQuestions.answer: In a raking grasp (7 months), the infant uses the whole hand like a rake to pull objects closer; in a pincer grip (9 months), the infant picks up small items (like cereal) precisely between thumb and forefinger.

inTextQuestions.question: Around what age does a toddler's vocabulary surge to roughly 7–9 new words per day, and what brain structure matures through puberty to support longer attention spans?
inTextQuestions.answer: Around 18 months of age. The Reticular Formation matures until puberty to regulate sustained and selective attention.

inTextQuestions.question: How do bilingual/multilingual children compare cognitively to monolingual children according to the course text?
inTextQuestions.answer: Bilingual and multilingual children are cognitively more proficient and develop a better understanding of language compared to monolingual children.

inTextQuestions.question: Distinguish between Sustained Attention, Selective Attention, and Divided Attention in childhood cognitive development.
inTextQuestions.answer: Sustained attention maintains focus on one task over a long period; Selective attention focuses on one task while ignoring distractions (e.g., TV); Divided attention multitasks two activities simultaneously without losing track of either.

saqs.question: Distinguish between gross motor skills and fine motor skills with four examples of each, and explain why hand-eye coordination matters for schooling.
saqs.answer: Gross motor skills use large trunk, arm, and leg muscles (walking, running, jumping, climbing, throwing/catching, pedalling). Fine motor skills use small hand/finger muscles (building block towers, jigsaw puzzles, tying shoelaces, cutting with scissors, clay modelling). Maturing small hand and eye muscles build hand-eye coordination, a prerequisite for holding a pencil properly and forming precise letters and numbers.

saqs.question: Summarize key developmental milestones across infancy at 3 months, 6 months, 9 months, and 12 months.
saqs.answer: 3 mos: smiles at voice, lifts head/chest prone, grasps toys, vowel sounds. 6 mos: sits briefly unsupported, recognizes own name, consonant/vowel babbling, laughs/cries emotionally. 9 mos: crawls, plays peekaboo/finds hidden toys, pincer grip, points. 12 mos: cruises/stands unsupported/takes 1–2 steps, says 1–2 simple words (hi/no/bye), uses spoon/comb clumsily.

saqs.question: Trace physical, mental, and emotional milestones in toddlerhood at 12–15 months, 18–24 months, and 24–36 months.
saqs.answer: 12–15 mos: stands alone, 4–6 words, object permanence, points for wants. 18–24 mos: runs/climbs steps/uses spoon, 20–50 words/stacks 6 blocks/sorts toys, asserts 'no'/tantrums/self-recognition/turn-taking. 24–36 mos: climbs well/puzzles/dresses self, speaks in sentences/imaginative play, knows boys from girls and shows personal preferences.

saqs.question: Compare Early Childhood (2–6 years) and Middle Childhood (6–11/13 years) in terms of physical growth, motor skills, attention, and thinking.
saqs.answer: Early childhood (2–6 yrs): refined locomotion/balance (skipping at 4), dramatic fine motor gains (buttons), symbolic thought, attention expands from 15–20 min (age 3) to 1+ hr (age 6). Middle childhood (6–11/13 yrs): slower steady growth until puberty, faster reaction time, copies diamonds/uses tools, systematic logical thinking about concrete objects (without abstract hypotheticals), hobbies, and stable sex-role identity.

saqs.question: Define Working Memory, Long-Term Memory, Auditory Processing, and Visual Processing, and list five psychosocial treatments used for childhood mental health concerns.
saqs.answer: Working memory retains information while actively using it (following multi-step instructions); Long-term memory stores past knowledge/formulas; Auditory processing analyses/blends sounds for reading; Visual processing interprets images, maps, and graphs. Psychosocial treatments: structured counselling, motivational enhancement, case management, care-coordination, psychotherapy, and relapse prevention.
